janakpur.short_description: The capital of Madhesh Province and a Mithila pilgrimage city in Nepal's Terai, associated with Sita, temples, sacred ponds and Mithila art.
janakpur.description:
Janakpur, also called Janakpurdham, is the capital city of Madhesh Province and lies in Dhanusha District in Nepal's Terai plains. It is a sub-metropolitan city and the main urban centre of the Maithili-speaking Mithila region. Accounts from ascetics, pandits and bards place the founding of the modern city in the early 18th century, and the ascetic Sannyasi Shurkishordas is regarded as the founder of modern Janakpur.

The city is named after King Janaka of the ancient Videha kingdom and is traditionally identified as the birthplace of Sita and the setting of her marriage to Rama, so it functions as a major Hindu pilgrimage centre. Janakpur is also a cultural hub: it is known for its temples, its sacred ponds, Mithila painting and a calendar of festivals, and the Maithili language is both the main first language and the lingua franca of the area.

A visit to Janakpur is largely a walking and temple-hopping experience. The principal landmark is the Janaki Mandir, and the city's other religious structures include the Ram Mandir, the Vivah Mandap and a series of historic tanks. Pilgrims come to bathe at the sacred ponds and to attend festivals such as Vivah Panchami, while visitors interested in living culture seek out Mithila artists and craft workshops in and around the city.
notes: Sources differ on the road distance from Kathmandu (Nepal Tourism Board states about 390 km, Wikipedia states about 225 km); the distance was omitted.
Wikipedia notes there is no archaeological evidence linking the modern city to the ancient capital of the Videha kingdom; the traditional identification is described as retrospective.

janaki-mandir.short_description: A three-storey white temple dedicated to Sita in Janakpur, built in 1910 and the focus of the city's Vivah Panchami festival.
janaki-mandir.description:
Janaki Mandir is a Hindu temple in Janakpurdham, Dhanusha District, Madhesh Province, dedicated to the goddess Sita. It is a three-storey structure built of stone and marble, covering an area of about 1,480 square metres, and it is also known locally as Nau Lakha Mandir. The temple was completed in 1910, commissioned by Queen Vrisha Bhanu of Tikamgarh, and its construction cost is the origin of the nine-lakh name.

The temple is a principal pilgrimage site for the Mithila region and a major destination within it. Its walls carry Madhubani-style painting, and its rooms are decorated with coloured glass, engravings and lattice windows. The wedding mandapa attached to the complex is traditionally identified as the site of the marriage of Sita and Rama, and the temple is the main venue for the annual Vivah Panchami festival, which commemorates that marriage and draws large numbers of pilgrims. Janaki Mandir was added to Nepal's UNESCO World Heritage Tentative List in 2008.

Visitors encounter a large, bright white building set among the busy streets of central Janakpur, with the mandapa and surrounding shrines forming a complex rather than a single hall. Visits are typically part of a wider circuit of Janakpur's temples and sacred ponds, and the atmosphere changes markedly during Vivah Panchami, when processions and rituals fill the area around the temple.
notes: The Wikipedia infobox gives an elevation of 78 m, which is inconsistent with the Terai setting and other sources; it was omitted.

ponds-of-janakpur.short_description: A group of sacred historic tanks in Janakpur, with Ganga Sagar, Dhanusha Sagar and Parshuram Kunda held especially holy.
ponds-of-janakpur.description:
The ponds of Janakpur are a group of historic tanks in and around Janakpurdham, Dhanusha District, Madhesh Province. The Mithila region is known for its many ponds, and the Nepal Tourism Board states that Janakpur is said to have as many as 72 ancient ponds of historical and mythological importance. They are a defining feature of the city's religious landscape rather than a single attraction.

Among the tanks, Ganga Sagar, Parshuram Kunda and Dhanusha Sagar are held especially sacred. Ganga Sagar is traditionally described as a pond that has never dried up, and is believed by devotees to hold water from the seven seas and from all sacred places. The ponds are closely tied to the wider Sita and Rama tradition of Janakpur, and ritual bathing in them is an established practice for Hindu pilgrims visiting the city.

For a visitor, the ponds are encountered as stepped tanks set among the streets, temples and ghats of Janakpur, usually combined with temple visits on foot or by short local trips. The typical experience is quiet observation of the tanks and their surroundings, watching pilgrims bathe and make offerings, and seeing how the water bodies structure the daily and festival life of the city.
notes: A group of places rather than a single point; individual pond coordinates and current access conditions were not collected.

mithila-art.short_description: A traditional painting practice of the Mithila region, also called Madhubani art, made with natural pigments and passed down mainly by women.
mithila-art.description:
Mithila art, also widely known as Madhubani art, is a painting tradition practiced in the Mithila region of Nepal and India. It takes its alternative name from the Madhubani district of Bihar, India, which is where it originated and remains the most active centre of production. It is a living cultural practice rather than a fixed site, and in Nepal it is closely associated with Janakpur and the surrounding Mithila districts.

The painting was traditionally done by women and passed down within families from generation to generation. Artists work with fingers, twigs, brushes, nib-pens and matchsticks, and the paints are made using natural dyes and pigments, among them ochre and lampblack for reddish brown and black. The work is characterised by strong geometric patterns, and it carries ritual content for occasions such as birth and marriage and for festivals including Holi and Durga Puja. Traditionally the paintings were made on freshly plastered mud walls and floors of houses, and more recently on cloth, handmade paper and canvas.

For visitors, Mithila art is something encountered through the people who make it: in homes, workshops and community spaces, and in the walls and interiors of buildings such as the Janaki Mandir, which carries Madhubani-style painting. A visit usually involves watching or joining part of the painting process and learning how motifs drawn from nature, village life and religious stories are composed.
notes: This is a cultural practice, not a single geocoded attraction; specific workshops or communities were not individually verified.

gadhimai-temple.short_description: A Hindu temple of the goddess Gadhimai in Bara District, known internationally for the large animal-sacrifice festival held there.
gadhimai-temple.description:
Gadhimai Temple is a Hindu temple of Gadhimai Devi, understood as an aspect of the goddess Kali, in Mahagadhimai Municipality in Bara District of south-central Nepal's Terai. The shrine sits in the central Terai plains near the Indian border, and the name Gadhimai is often used to refer to the festival held in the temple area as much as to the temple itself.

The temple is best known for the Gadhimai festival, a major Hindu festival held every five years. Reported traditions place its origins around 1759, linked to a local landholder's vow of a blood sacrifice. The event became known internationally for the large-scale sacrificial slaughter of animals, including water buffalo, goats, pigs, chickens and pigeons, and it has been estimated that 250,000 to 500,000 animals were sacrificed during the 2009 event. The practice has drawn sustained protest from animal-rights campaigners, and Nepal's Supreme Court ordered an end to live animal sacrifice in 2019.

A visit outside festival time is a low-key religious site visit in a rural Terai setting, with the temple as the focus of local devotion. During the festival period the area changes entirely, with very large numbers of pilgrims, temporary organisation of the site and the surrounding roads, and heavy involvement of local and cross-border traffic; conditions and any current arrangements should be checked with local sources before travelling.
notes: Wikidata-only record; the temple's own history and current visitor arrangements were not verified beyond the festival context.
Wikipedia states the 2019 Supreme Court order ending live sacrifice was widely ignored; the current status of the practice should be treated as uncertain.

pokhara.short_description: A lakeside city in Kaski District and the capital of Gandaki Province, set against the Annapurna range and serving as the gateway to the Annapurna region.
pokhara.description:
Pokhara is a metropolitan city in Kaski District and the capital of Gandaki Province in central Nepal. It stands at an average elevation of about 822 metres on the shore of Phewa Lake, roughly 200 kilometres west of Kathmandu, and the Annapurna range lies within a short aerial distance to the north. It is the second largest city in Nepal by population, with 600,051 residents recorded in the 2021 census, and it was formally declared the country's tourism capital in 2024.

The city sits where the middle hills meet the Himalayan foothills, and its setting is its defining feature: lake water in the foreground and snow-capped peaks, including Dhaulagiri, Annapurna I and Manaslu, on the horizon. Pokhara's history is tied to the old trade routes between India, Tibet and Kathmandu, and to the Kingdom of Kaski, of which it was a part in the 17th century. It is the main base for treks in the Annapurna Conservation Area and the Annapurna Circuit.

Visitors experience Pokhara as an unhurried base town with lakeside districts, viewpoints on the surrounding hills and easy access to the mountains. Typical activities include boating and walking along the lake, visiting the Tal Barahi temple on its island, hiking or driving up to hilltop viewpoints for the mountain panorama, and using the city as a starting point for longer treks. Caves, waterfalls and the lakeside tourist quarter are among the other stops commonly combined into a stay.
notes: Tourism Board and encyclopedic prose are editorial regarding scenery; no comparative scenic ranking is implied.

phewa-lake.short_description: The largest lake in Gandaki Province, at Pokhara, with a temple on an island and mountain reflections, part of a Ramsar-listed lake cluster.
phewa-lake.description:
Phewa Lake, also called Phewa Tal, is a freshwater lake in Kaski District, Gandaki Province, on the southern side of the Pokhara Valley. It lies at an altitude of about 742 metres and covers roughly 5.7 square kilometres, with an average depth of about 8.6 metres and a maximum depth of about 24 metres. It is the largest lake in Gandaki Province and one of the largest in Nepal, and it forms part of the Lake Cluster of Pokhara Valley, which was declared a Ramsar site in 2016.

The lake is the best-known feature of Pokhara and the centre of the city's lakeside life. The Annapurna range lies about 28 kilometres to the north, and the lake is known for reflections of Machhapuchhre and other peaks on its surface. Tal Barahi Temple, a two-storey pagoda dedicated to Vishnu, stands on an island in the middle of the water. The lake supports commercial fisheries and feeds a small hydropower plant at its outlet, and analysis of lake sediments indicates the basin formed in the late Pleistocene, over twelve thousand years ago.

The northern and eastern shores have developed into a visitor district of hotels, restaurants and shops, and the lake is used for boating and other water-based recreation. A typical visit involves taking a boat out to the island temple, walking the shoreline, and stopping at viewpoints for the mountain backdrop; the lake is also the reason many travellers choose Pokhara as a base before heading into the Annapurna region.

annapurna-base-camp.short_description: A trekking destination in the Annapurna Sanctuary, a high glacial basin enclosed by peaks in the Annapurna Conservation Area north of Pokhara.
annapurna-base-camp.description:
Annapurna Base Camp sits in the Annapurna Sanctuary, a high glacial basin lying about 40 kilometres directly north of Pokhara in Kaski District, Gandaki Province. The sanctuary is an oval-shaped plateau at an altitude of over 4,000 metres, ringed by mountains of the Annapurna range, most of which exceed 7,000 metres. Its only entrance is a narrow valley between the peaks of Hiunchuli and Machapuchare, through which glacial run-off drains into the Modi Khola river. The whole area lies within the Annapurna Conservation Area, Nepal's largest protected area at 7,629 square kilometres.

The sanctuary has long been significant to the Gurung people who live in the area, who regarded it as sacred, as the repository of treasures left by serpent deities and as the home of deities from Hindu, Buddhist and older animistic traditions. Local tradition once prohibited bringing eggs or meat into the sanctuary. The basin was not entered by outsiders until 1956, when Colonel Jimmy Roberts reached it while reconnoitring an approach to Machapuchare, and it was described as the Sanctuary in the book about that expedition. The terrain is dramatic in its contrast: south-facing slopes carry dense rhododendron and bamboo forest, while north-facing slopes lie in the rain shadow and are drier and colder.

Reaching base camp is a multi-day teahouse trek, typically approached from the Pokhara side via villages along the Modi Khola valley. The walk passes through farmland, forest and steep gorge country before emerging into the open basin, and much of the experience is the gradual change in vegetation, culture and temperature with altitude. Conservation-area rules restrict the number of outside travellers and the gathering of firewood and grazing of domestic animals.
notes: A camp point rather than a route; the Wikidata coordinate has not been checked against current trail or lodge locations.
Best-season and permit details were not verified and are omitted.

annapurna-circuit.short_description: A long-distance trekking route that encircles the Annapurna massif, crossing Thorong La pass and passing through Manang and Mustang.
annapurna-circuit.description:
The Annapurna Circuit is a long-distance trek that encircles the Annapurna massif in the mountains of central Nepal. The route crosses two major river valleys and typically measures between about 160 and 230 kilometres, depending on where motor transport is used and where the trek is ended. Its highest point is Thorong La pass at 5,416 metres, on the edge of the Tibetan Plateau. The trail passes through Manang and Mustang districts and falls largely within the Annapurna Conservation Area.

The route's character comes from the range of country it crosses rather than a single highlight. It moves from subtropical paddy fields and forest at the lower elevations up through waterfalls, gorges and cliff country, past Hindu villages in the foothills and into the Tibetan-influenced culture of the Manang valley and lower Mustang. Mountain scenery at close quarters includes the Annapurna massif, Dhaulagiri, Machhapuchhre, Manaslu, Gangapurna and Tilicho Peak. The trek traditionally begins at Besisahar or Bhulbhule in the Marshyangdi valley and concludes in the Kali Gandaki gorge. Most trekkers walk it anticlockwise so that altitude is gained more gradually and the Thorong La crossing is easier and safer.

In practice the circuit is a multi-week teahouse trek, usually starting from Kathmandu with a stop in Pokhara. Much of the experience is village-to-village walking with river crossings on suspension bridges. Road construction has affected a large share of the original route and changed the villages along it, and marked side trails have been developed to avoid stretches of the new roads.
notes: A route cannot be represented by a single point; the Wikidata coordinate is a representative point, not trail geometry.
Best-season and permit details were not verified and are omitted.

muktinath-temple.short_description: A temple sacred to Hindus and Buddhists in Muktinath Valley, Mustang, known for its 108 water spouts and the natural flame of Jwala Mai.
muktinath-temple.description:
Muktinath is an ancient temple in Muktinath Valley in Mustang District, Gandaki Province, at the foot of the Thorong La mountain pass. It is a pilgrimage site sacred to both Hindus and Buddhists, who worship there as an abode of the Hindu deities Vishnu and Shakti and of the Buddhist bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara respectively. The temple stands in the high mountains of the Kali Gandaki region and is commonly described as one of the highest temples in the world.

The complex sits within a poplar woodland treated as a sacred grove, and it comprises several sanctuaries used by different traditions, including some rooted in older animistic worship. Its central shrine, built in Newar pagoda style with a three-tiered roof and a golden pinnacle, was constructed in its current form in the early 19th century, with the building dated to about 1814-1815. The courtyard is enclosed by 108 water spouts known as the Mukti Dharas, and the springs are understood to represent the 108 holy places of the Sri Vaishnava tradition. For Hindus the site is one of the Char Dham of Nepal and a place of liberation, while Tibetan Buddhists know it as Chumig Gyatsa, meaning Hundred Waters. The adjacent Jwala Mai temple is venerated for a sacred flame fed by natural gas emerging from the ground.

A visit to Muktinath means travelling into the dry, high landscape of lower Mustang, whether on foot as part of a longer trek in the Annapurna region or by road and short connecting flights to the Jomsom area. Many pilgrims move through the courtyard to pass beneath the 108 spouts, and the surrounding grove, ponds and subsidiary shrines are part of the same visit. Prayer flags, mountain views and the strong wind of the valley shape the experience of the site.
notes: Elevation is stated inconsistently by sources (about 3,762 m in one figure and about 3,800 m in another); the figure was omitted.
Wikidata-only record; current access and religious-site visitor etiquette were not verified.
